forbidden_claims.statement_nl: Let [m]_q = (1−q^m)/(1−q), let (a;q)_k = ∏_{j=0}^{k−1} (1−aq^j), let (a,b,c;q)_k = (a;q)_k (b;q)_k (c;q)_k, and let Φ_n(q) be the nth cyclotomic polynomial. Prove that for positive integers d and r with gcd(d,r)=1 and r ≤ d, and for every integer n > 1 with n ≡ 1 mod 2d, we have Σ_{k=0}^{n−1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k^2 q^(k(d−dk−2r)/2) / (q^{2d};q^{2d})_k ≡ [rn]_q q^(r(1−n)/2) mod [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2.

payload.statement_nl: Let [m]_q=(1-q^m)/(1-q), let Φ_n(q) be the nth cyclotomic polynomial, define M_n(q):=[n]_q Φ_n(q)^2, and define U_{d,n}(q):=∏_{j=1}^{n-1}(1+q^{dj}). Suppose d and r are positive integers with gcd(d,r)=1 and r <= d, and suppose n>1 satisfies n ≡ 1 mod 2d. Then n is odd and gcd(n,2d)=1. Consequently, if ζ is any complex number with ζ^n=1 and ζ ≠ 1, then U_{d,n}(ζ) ≠ 0. In particular gcd(U_{d,n}(q),M_n(q))=1 in Z[q].

result_payload.proof_nl:
Only the congruence n ≡ 1 mod 2d is needed in the argument below; the hypotheses involving r are harmless but not used.

Because n ≡ 1 mod 2d, there is an integer t with n = 1 + 2dt. Hence n is odd. Also, if g is any common divisor of n and 2d, then g divides 2dt = n - 1 as well, so g divides n - (n - 1) = 1. Therefore gcd(n,2d) = 1.

Now let ζ be any complex number with ζ^n = 1 and ζ ≠ 1. Suppose, for contradiction, that U_{d,n}(ζ) = 0. Since
U_{d,n}(ζ) = ∏_{j=1}^{n-1} (1 + ζ^{dj}),
there must exist some j with 1 ≤ j ≤ n - 1 such that 1 + ζ^{dj} = 0. Thus ζ^{dj} = -1. Raising both sides to the nth power gives
1 = (ζ^{dj})^n = (-1)^n = -1,
because n is odd. This is impossible. Hence every factor 1 + ζ^{dj} is nonzero, and therefore U_{d,n}(ζ) ≠ 0.

It remains to prove gcd(U_{d,n}(q), M_n(q)) = 1 in Z[q]. Suppose instead that there exists a nonconstant common divisor H(q) ∈ Z[q] of U_{d,n}(q) and M_n(q). Viewing H as a polynomial in C[q], it is still nonconstant, so by the fundamental theorem of algebra it has some complex root α. Then H(α) = 0. Since H divides M_n(q) = [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2, we have M_n(α) = 0, so either [n]_q evaluated at q = α is 0, or Φ_n(α) = 0.

If [n]_q evaluated at q = α is 0, then using the geometric-sum identity [n]_q = 1 + q + ··· + q^{n-1}, we get [n]_1 = n ≠ 0, so α ≠ 1. Also,
(α - 1)[n]_q|_{q=α} = α^n - 1,
so α^n - 1 = 0. Thus α^n = 1 and α ≠ 1.

If Φ_n(α) = 0, then by the defining property of the nth cyclotomic polynomial, α is a primitive nth root of unity. In particular α^n = 1 and α ≠ 1.

So in either case α is a nontrivial nth root of unity. By the previous paragraph, U_{d,n}(α) ≠ 0. But H divides U_{d,n}, and H(α) = 0, so necessarily U_{d,n}(α) = 0, a contradiction.

Therefore U_{d,n}(q) and M_n(q) have no nonconstant common divisor in Z[q]. Equivalently, gcd(U_{d,n}(q), M_n(q)) = 1 in Z[q].
result_payload.proof_summary: From n ≡ 1 mod 2d we get n = 1 + 2dt, so n is odd, and any common divisor of n and 2d divides 1; hence gcd(n,2d)=1. Then no factor 1+ζ^{dj} can vanish for an nth root ζ, because that would force (-1)^n=1. Finally, any nonconstant common divisor of U_{d,n} and M_n would have a complex root α; since M_n(α)=0, α is a nontrivial nth root of unity, but U_{d,n} does not vanish at such points, contradiction.

used_external_facts: Fundamental theorem of algebra: every nonconstant polynomial over C has a complex root.
Defining property of the nth cyclotomic polynomial: its complex roots are the primitive nth roots of unity.
